summary: Adds versioning to WebDAV with new HTTP methods, headers and resource types, so tools can track revisions of web resources. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of saving each draft of an essay instead of overwriting it. This lets web file sharing remember every version.

questions: what does the checkout method do in webdav
subtitle: How WebDAV remembers every saved state of a web resource, with check-out, check-in, labels, merges and baselines.

tldr.problem: WebDAV lets clients edit resources on a web server, but there was no standard way to keep the history of those resources, name past states, or let several people work in parallel.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds new methods (such as VERSION-CONTROL, CHECKOUT, CHECKIN, LABEL and MERGE), headers, properties and reports. A resource under version control gets a version history, and each saved state becomes an immutable version with its own URL.
tldr.outcome: A server can support any combination of features, from simple linear versioning to workspaces, baselines and activities. Basic servers are advised to implement one of three packages so clients stay simple.

today: RFC 3253 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2518 and RFC 2616.

sections.title: Why Version the Web
sections.content:
RFC 3253 defines the WebDAV versioning extensions to HTTP/1.1. Versioning is about tracking and accessing the history of important states of a web resource, such as a standalone web page. The RFC lists two benefits: a resource gets an explicit history and a persistent identity across its states, and each state gets a stable name that annotation and link servers can point to.

The design builds on WebDAV (RFC 2518) and HTTP (RFC 2616). All method behavior from those documents continues to hold, so clients that know nothing about versioning can still work with a versioning server.

The RFC splits the work into basic versioning and advanced versioning, which adds parallel development and configuration management of sets of resources. An implementer interested only in the basics can skip Sections 10 to 14.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally saving a file wipes out the old one. Versioning is like keeping every old copy, each with its own label, so you can always go back.

sections.title: Versions, Histories and Check-Out
sections.content:
A version-controlled resource is a normal resource that has been put under version control. It is either checked in or checked out, and the version control constraints apply only while it is checked in. A version is a resource that holds a copy of one state (content and dead properties). The server gives each new version a new URL that is never reused, and a version never changes.

All versions of one resource live in a version history. When a resource is checked out and then checked in, the version that was checked out becomes the predecessor of the new one. A new version can have several predecessors, which makes it a merge. Two successors of one version make a fork. A server may restrict history to a straight line, but a good client should be ready for forks and merges.

A VERSION-CONTROL request does three things: it creates a version history, creates a first version that copies the resource, and turns the resource into a version-controlled resource with a DAV:checked-in property pointing at that version. The resource keeps its URL. A version captures content and dead properties, but not live properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time you finish a draft, it goes on a shelf as its own book that can never be changed. The shelf is the history, and the draft on your desk is the one you can keep editing.

sections.title: Basic Methods and Auto-Versioning
sections.content:
To change a version-controlled resource with PUT or PROPPATCH, a client first sends CHECKOUT, which adds a DAV:checked-out property and removes DAV:checked-in. CHECKIN creates a new version copied from the checked-out resource. UNCHECKOUT cancels the checkout and restores the earlier state.

The DAV:auto-version property lets a server handle clients that know nothing about versioning. Its values are DAV:checkout-checkin, DAV:checkout-unlocked-checkin, DAV:checkout and DAV:locked-checkout, which differ in when the server checks the resource out and back in, and how write locks affect that.

Information that needs parameters comes from the REPORT method. The DAV:version-tree report returns properties of every version in a history, and DAV:expand-property can follow property links. Failed preconditions and postconditions are answered with 403 (Forbidden) or 409 (Conflict) and a named XML element inside DAV:error.
sections.plainLanguage: To change a page you borrow it, edit it, then hand it back and it becomes the newest copy. Some servers do the borrowing and returning for you automatically.

sections.title: Features and Packages
sections.content:
Versioning is split into features that a server may combine: version-control, checkout-in-place, version-history, workspace, update, label and working-resource. The version-control feature MUST be supported if any other is. A server announces features by listing them in the DAV header of an OPTIONS response.

To keep clients simple, a basic versioning server SHOULD support one of three packages: core-versioning (version-control), basic-server-workspace (version-control, workspace, version-history, checkout), or basic-client-workspace (version-control, working-resource, update, label). In the server package all state stays on the server and each client gets a workspace resource. In the client package the client keeps its own state locally and uses server-side working resources to prepare consistent updates. A server supporting both workspace packages interoperates with all basic versioning clients.

Related methods include MKWORKSPACE to create a workspace, UPDATE to set a checked-in resource to a chosen version, and LABEL to add, set or remove a label on a version. A Label request header, for example Label: release%20B.3, makes methods such as GET apply to the version that label selects.
sections.plainLanguage: The server offers a menu of extras, like a pizza place. The RFC suggests three ready-made combos so every customer and kitchen understand each other.

sections.title: Advanced Features
sections.content:
The advanced features cover parallel development and configuration management.

  • MERGE merges a version into a version-controlled resource. If the server cannot do it automatically, the source URL goes into DAV:merge-set and the client must fix up the content, then move it into the predecessor set. The server MUST fail a CHECKIN while the merge set is not empty.
  • Baselines capture the checked-in version of every version-controlled member of a collection's configuration. BASELINE-CONTROL places a collection under baseline control.
  • Activities are created with MKACTIVITY and select the versions that belong to one logical change, on a single line of descent per version history.
  • Version-controlled collections record only binding names and version histories of their members, so changing one member does not force a new version of every parent collection.
sections.plainLanguage: Merging is combining two people's edits into one. A baseline is a photo of a whole folder at one moment. An activity is a sticky note that groups all the edits for one job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All WebDAV security considerations from RFC 2518 also apply. Versioning helps in one way: immutable versions and a history that records when changes were made, and by whom, give an audit trail when requests are authenticated.

It also raises risks. Links between versions increase the need for access control: someone who can see the history of a public resource might find later versions meant to stay private. Clients should expect a mix of 200 and 403 responses when reading versioning properties. Server-generated version URLs can be obscured, though the RFC admits obscurity is not real security. Auto-versioning can create very many versions, for example from an aggressive auto-save, which may exhaust storage; servers can use delta storage or limit auto-versioning to locking clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping every old draft helps you see who changed what, but you also have to lock the cupboard, or someone could read drafts you wanted private.
